Error:

docs.title: Users
docs.text:
List users:

Create user with grants:

CREATE USER 'username'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY 'password';
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, CREATE, DROP, INDEX, ALTER,
  CREATE TEMPORARY TABLES ON dbname.* TO 'username'@'%' IDENTIFIED BY 'password';

Full admin user:

CREATE USER 'admin'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY 'password';
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON *.* TO 'admin'@'localhost' WITH GRANT OPTION;
CREATE USER 'admin'@'%' IDENTIFIED BY 'password';
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON *.* TO 'admin'@'%' WITH GRANT OPTION;
FLUSH PRIVILEGES;

Change password:

ALTER USER 'user'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY 'new_password';
FLUSH PRIVILEGES;

Delete user:

DROP USER 'user'@'host';

docs.title: dns
docs.text: Domain Name System — translates human-readable names to IP addresses. The phone book of the internet.

docs.title: How resolution works
docs.text:
```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant B as Browser participant R as Resolver8.8.8.8 participant Root as Root NS. participant TLD as TLD NS.com participant Auth as Authoritative NSexample.com

B->>B: local cache / /etc/hosts
B->>R: who is example.com?
R->>Root: query example.com
Root-->>R: ask .com TLD
R->>TLD: query example.com
TLD-->>R: ask ns1.example.com
R->>Auth: query example.com
Auth-->>R: 93.184.216.34
R-->>B: 93.184.216.34

```

docs.title: Record types
docs.text: Type Purpose Example A Name → IPv4 example.com → 93.184.216.34 AAAA Name → IPv6 example.com → 2606:2800:220:1:... CNAME Alias → another name www.example.com → example.com MX Mail server example.com → mail.example.com (pri 10) TXT Arbitrary text SPF, DKIM, domain verification NS Name server example.com → ns1.example.com SOA Zone authority Serial, refresh, retry, expire SRV Service location _http._tcp.example.com → ... PTR Reverse lookup (IP → name) 34.216.184.93 → example.com

docs.title: Diagnostic commands
docs.text:
# Basic lookup
dig example.com
dig example.com +short

# Specific record type
dig MX example.com
dig TXT example.com
dig AAAA example.com

# Query specific nameserver
dig @8.8.8.8 example.com

# Trace full resolution path
dig +trace example.com

# Reverse lookup
dig -x 93.184.216.34

# Short answer with nslookup
nslookup example.com
host example.com

docs.title: Local resolution
docs.text:
# Check local resolver config
cat /etc/resolv.conf

# Check hosts file
cat /etc/hosts

# Check nsswitch order

docs.title: Common issues
docs.text:
Resolution fails locally but works from outside: - Check /etc/resolv.conf — wrong nameserver? - Check /etc/nsswitch.conf — is files before dns? - CoreDNS/kube-dns issues in Kubernetes

TTL too high after DNS change: 

# Check current TTL
dig example.com | grep -E '^\w'
# Lower TTL before migration, wait for old TTL to expire

docs.title: osi_model
docs.text: Open Systems Interconnection — a reference model for how protocols communicate over a network. Seven layers, bottom to top.

docs.title: Layers
docs.text: # Layer Function Protocols / Examples 7 Application User-facing services HTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNS 6 Presentation Data format, encryption TLS/SSL, JPEG, ASCII 5 Session Connection management NetBIOS, RPC 4 Transport Reliable delivery TCP, UDP 3 Network Routing, addressing IP, ICMP, ARP 2 Data Link Frames, MAC addressing Ethernet, Wi-Fi, PPP 1 Physical Bits on wire Cables, hubs, signals

docs.title: How to remember
docs.text:
Layer 1 → 7: Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away

Layer 7 → 1: All People Seem To Need Data Processing

docs.title: Troubleshooting by layer
docs.text:
When diagnosing an issue, work from bottom to top:

  1. Physical — is the cable plugged in? Is the link up? 
    ip link
ethtool eth0
  2. Data Link — do we have a MAC address? ARP working? 
    ip neigh
arp -a
  3. Network — do we have an IP? Can we reach the gateway? 
    ip addr
ping -c 3 $gateway
traceroute $destination
  4. Transport — is the port open? Is something listening? 
    ss -tulpn | grep $port
nc -zv $host $port
  5. Application — does the service respond correctly? 
    curl -v https://$host
dig $domain

docs.title: tcp_ip_model
docs.text: The practical model. Four layers instead of seven. This is what the internet actually runs on.

docs.title: Layers
docs.text: # TCP/IP Layer OSI Equivalent Protocols 4 Application 5, 6, 7 HTTP, DNS, SMTP, SSH, FTP 3 Transport 4 TCP, UDP 2 Internet 3 IP, ICMP, ARP 1 Network Access 1, 2 Ethernet, Wi-Fi

docs.title: TCP vs UDP
docs.text: TCP UDP Connection Connection-oriented (3-way handshake) Connectionless Reliability Guaranteed delivery, ordering Best effort, no guarantees Speed Slower (overhead) Faster (no overhead) Use cases HTTP, SSH, FTP, SMTP DNS, DHCP, streaming, gaming

docs.title: TCP three-way handshake
docs.text:
Client → Server:  SYN         (I want to connect)
Server → Client:  SYN-ACK     (OK, acknowledged)
Client → Server:  ACK          (Confirmed, let's go)

docs.title: tls
docs.text: Transport Layer Security — encrypts data in transit. Successor to SSL. When people say "SSL" they almost always mean TLS.

docs.title: SSL vs TLS
docs.text:
SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) was the original protocol. Deprecated due to vulnerabilities. TLS (Transport Layer Security) is the modern replacement.

Version Status SSL 2.0, 3.0 Deprecated, insecure TLS 1.0, 1.1 Deprecated since 2020 TLS 1.2 Widely used, still secure TLS 1.3 Current, fastest, most secure

docs.title: TLS handshake (simplified)
docs.text:
Client → Server:  ClientHello     (supported ciphers, TLS version)
Server → Client:  ServerHello     (chosen cipher, certificate)
Client:           Verify cert     (check CA chain, expiry, domain)
Client → Server:  Key exchange    (shared secret via asymmetric crypto)
Both:             Derive keys     (symmetric encryption begins)

TLS 1.3 reduced the handshake from 2 round-trips to 1.

docs.title: Certificate inspection
docs.text:
# Check remote certificate
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -text

# Expiry date only
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -dates

# Check with curl
curl -vI https://example.com 2>&1 | grep -E 'expire|subject|issuer'

docs.title: Self-signed certificate (dev/testing)
docs.text:
openssl req -x509 -nodes -days 365 -newkey rsa:2048 \
  -keyout tls.key -out tls.crt \
  -subj "/CN=localhost"

docs.title: Kubernetes TLS secret
docs.text:
kubectl create secret tls my-tls-secret \
  --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key -n $ns

docs.title: Common issues
docs.text:
Certificate expired: - Check with openssl s_client above - In Kubernetes: check cert-manager logs, Certificate and CertificateRequest resources

ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID: - Self-signed cert or missing intermediate CA in chain - Chain must include: leaf cert → intermediate(s) → root CA

TLS version mismatch: 

# Test specific TLS version
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -tls1_2
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -tls1_3
